verdict: 2026-07-26 08:29 PDT — The temp-directory and log-sanitization designs are small, idiomatic, and consistent with the repository. The rate-limiter library and middleware placement are also appropriate, but the proposed client-IP mechanism rests on an undocumented Railway proxy assumption and should be redesigned before implementation. AC4 also remains contingent on Thomas’s explicit disposition.

findings.title: The per-IP limiter relies on an unverified proxy contract
findings.claim: `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` assumes exactly one proxy hop supplying `X-Forwarded-For`. [Railway’s current networking specification](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits) documents `X-Real-IP` as the client-IP header, not `X-Forwarded-For`; therefore the default limiter key may collapse users into a proxy-wide bucket. Conversely, an incorrect numeric hop count can admit spoofed addresses. [Express explicitly requires numeric trust depth to match every deployment path](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/behind-proxies.html). Because `trust proxy` also changes application-wide request semantics inherited by future routes, this is a cross-cutting assumption rather than a limiter-local detail.
findings.alternative: Keep Express’s default trust setting and give this limiter a narrow `keyGenerator` that validates Railway’s documented `X-Real-IP`, normalizes it with `express-rate-limit`’s `ipKeyGenerator`, and falls back safely to the socket address. Test that repeated requests from one valid forwarded IP are limited while another IP retains its own bucket. Alternatively, retain numeric trust only after live evidence establishes Railway’s complete forwarding chain and add a representative proxy-header test.
findings.win: Prevents the intended per-IP control from becoming either one shared bucket or a spoofable no-op, removes an application-wide proxy setting, and centralizes Railway-specific identity handling inside the one component that needs it.

findings.title: AC4 still has no selected implementation path
findings.claim: The sketch remains conditional on Q1: dismissal produces no code change, while narrowing the boot diagnostic changes `index.js` or `oauth.js`. Until Thomas selects one, there is no complete design that can satisfy AC4 or the stated zero-alert outcome.
findings.alternative: Record Thomas’s explicit choice before implementation. Dismissal is a defensible false-positive disposition for the high-entropy truncated fingerprint; if code-only resolution is preferred, remove the secret-derived component at the boot-log call boundary and preserve the existing fingerprint helper for deliberate diagnostics.
findings.win: Eliminates an unresolved branch in the build plan and ensures the implementation and verification path for alert #2 are unambiguous.

findings.title: The 300-per-minute production ceiling is not yet justified
findings.locus: reviews/codeql-security-fixes.md — Open question Q2 / Design sketch #1
findings.claim: A per-IP quota is shared by users behind the same corporate NAT, while this no-cache SPA can consume several requests per load. The proposed tests prove middleware operation but cannot establish that 300 requests per minute avoids throttling legitimate concurrent Zoom users.
findings.alternative: Choose the default from the built client’s request fan-out and an explicit expected number of concurrent users per egress IP, then record that capacity calculation. Keep the injectable tiny ceiling for behavioral tests.
findings.win: Turns an arbitrary availability boundary into a reviewable capacity assumption and avoids production 429s for legitimate users sharing an enterprise network.
